name: Executive order of January 5, 1882 setting apart the Uncompahgre Reservation in Utah
nations: Ute Indian Tribe of the Uintah and Ouray Reservation (Uncompahgre, formerly Tabeguache, Band)
promises: Not a treaty: the President set apart a reserve in eastern Utah for the occupancy of the Uncompahgre Utes, running from township 6 south along the Uintah reservation line and the Green River to the third standard parallel south and the Colorado line (Royce). Royce records it as the present Uncompahgre reserve.
The Ute Indian Tribe says the order carried out the promise of the 1880 Act, ratifying the Ute agreement, of a new homeland for the Uncompahgre Band in Colorado or Utah.

breaches.what: The Ute Indian Tribe says the United States violated the 1880 Act and the executive order creating the Uncompahgre Reservation: it let non-Indian stockmen crowd out the Band's herds, sought oil and minerals there, and handed management of its lands and minerals to the Bureau of Land Management without approval from Congress.

breaches.quote: The United States promised us a new homeland in Colorado or Utah.

breaches.what: The Uncompahgre Band claimed before the Indian Claims Commission that it was the only Ute band not given a reservation under the 1880 agreement; the claim was settled by compromise for $300,000 without a ruling on the merits.
breaches.whoFoundIt: Indian Claims Commission, Ute Indian Tribe (Uncompahgre Band) v. United States, Docket 349, findings on stipulated settlement (February 18, 1965)

source.publisher: Indian Claims Commission Decisions, Oklahoma State University Library

landTaken: The Tribe's 2018 suits describe the historic Uncompahgre Reservation as about 1.8 million acres (Salt Lake Tribune, March 13, 2018); news reports of the 2026 ruling describe the claim as 1.5 million to 2 million acres. No acreage was found in the order or in Royce.
compensation: The Uncompahgre Band's Commission claim (Docket 349) was settled for $300,000 in 1965, a compromise, not a finding. No other payment for the reservation lands was found.
today: On July 31, 2026 the D.C. Circuit upheld the Interior Department's refusal to restore the lands under the Indian Reorganization Act, a ruling against the Tribe. FOX 13 reports a companion suit for compensation in the Court of Federal Claims was stayed pending that appeal.

nationVoice.summary: The Tribe says the United States promised the Uncompahgre Band a new homeland and then broke the 1880 Act and the order creating the reservation, and it went to court to hold the United States to those promises.

openQuestions: The Act of June 7, 1897 that allotted the reservation and opened the rest was not opened; reports of it come from search results only and are left out.

The D.C. Circuit opinion was read only in an excerpt; its holding is taken from that excerpt (Interior and the district court found the lands not eligible) and from FOX 13. The full opinion should be read, and the status of the Court of Federal Claims case checked.
The Tenth Circuit's rulings in Ute Indian Tribe v. Utah on whether the Uncompahgre Reservation was diminished were not opened; they would go in today, not breaches, unless they found a wrong.
utetribe.com returned a bot check on 2026-11-08, so the Tribe's own pages were not read; its voice here is its 2021 news release.

Audit 2026-11-08: removed the 2026 D.C. Circuit decision from breaches. It is a ruling against the Tribe (Interior found the lands not eligible for restoration), so under the rules it belongs in today, where it already is. Status unchanged (contested on the Tribe's statement and the Docket 349 compromise).

plain.promised: Not a treaty. In 1882 the President set apart a reservation in eastern Utah for the Uncompahgre Utes. The Ute Indian Tribe says this was the new homeland the United States promised.
plain.happened: The Tribe says the United States let others use and take the land and handed it to the Bureau of Land Management. No court or claims commission finding of a breach was found; a 1965 claim was settled.
plain.today: The Band settled its claim for $300,000 in 1965. In July 2026 an appeals court ruled against the Tribe's bid to restore the lands.
